Nicolaus Copernicus developed his heliocentric theory in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, when European politics was fractured by dynastic rivalry, religious reform, and imperial ambition.
The Polish kingdom enjoyed a stable, semi-elective monarchy, while the Holy Roman Empire remained a contested arena of Catholic authority, powerful magnates, and growing Reformation tensions.
Intellectual life shifted between late medieval scholasticism, humanist renewal, and Church insistence that Ptolemaic geocentrism fit orthodox cosmology.
Although his arrangement might appear cactiform to modern viewers, the political climate permitted cautious publication, manuscript circulation, and guarded scholarly debate.
